title: Song of the Lovestruck Widow
text:
Oh, I know I must not confess
that I tremble when his hand touches me.
Oh, what has happened to me
that I pray he will seduce me.
Oh, not a hundred horses could drag me into sin!
If only I did not desire him so much!


If I resist love so fiercely,
I have really resisted only at heart
because I know that if I were before him in my nightgown
he would leave me without even my shirt.
As if my reproaches mattered to him!
If only I did not desire him so much!


I doubt he is worth as much as I am
and that for him this is true love.
When all my savings have been spent,
will he throw the contraption in the trash?
Oh, now I know why I resisted him so much!
If only I did not desire him so much!


If I had two fingers' worth of sense,
I would never have granted him what, alas, he asked of me,
but would have beaten him soundly
as soon as he came too close, as he did.
Oh, I wish he would go to hell!
(If only I did not desire him so much!)
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The repeated refrain, speaker's self-reproach, and colloquial sexual bargaining are preserved.

title: The Prostitute's Song
text:
1

My lords, at seventeen
I came to the market of love
and learned a great deal.

There was much that was bad,
but that was the game.

Though there were things that did bother me
(after all, I too am a person).

Thank God everything passes quickly,
grief included; love as well.

Where are last night's tears?
Where is last year's snow?


2

Of course, as the years go by, one goes
lighter to the market of love
and embraces them by the herd.

But feelings
become surprisingly cold
when they are rationed so carefully
(after all, no supply lasts forever).

Thank God everything passes quickly,
grief included; love as well.

Where are last night's tears?
Where is last year's snow?


3

And even if you learn the trade well
at the fair of love,
turning pleasure into small change
is never easy.

But still, you manage it.

Though you grow old in the meantime
(after all, one is not always seventeen).

Thank God everything passes quickly,
grief included; love as well.

Where are last night's tears?
Where is last year's snow?
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The numbered structure, refrain, market and fair metaphors, and deliberately plain register are preserved.

title: Woman's Song
text:
1. At night beside the river, in the dark heart of the bushes,
sometimes I see her face again, the face of the woman I loved: my
woman, who died.

2. It was many years ago, and at times I know nothing of her anymore, the one
who once was everything, but everything withers.

3. And she was in me like a little juniper in the steppes of
Mongolia, concave, with the pale yellow sky and its great sadness.

4. We lived in a black hut beside the river; mosquitoes
used to pierce her white body, and I read the newspaper
seven times or said: “Your hair is a dirty color.” Or: “You have no heart.”

5. But one day, while I was washing my shirt in the
hut, she came to the door and looked at me and wanted to leave.

6. And the one who had beaten her until he was tired said: “My angel.”

7. And the one who had told her “I love you” led her outside and,
laughing, looked at the air and praised the good weather and took her hand.

8. Once they were outside, in the open air, and the hut was
deserted, he shut the door and sat down behind the newspaper.

9. Since then I have not seen her again, and all that remained of her was the little cry she gave when in the morning she returned to the door that
was already closed.

10. Now the hut has rotted and my chest is stuffed with
newspaper, and at night, lying beside the river in the
dark heart of the bushes, I remember her.

11. The wind carries the smell of grass in her hair and the water cries out endlessly asking God for calm, and in my tongue I have a bitter taste.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering, not from Brecht's German original. The numbered confession, repeated newspaper image, violence, and final bitter taste are preserved.

title: Villainous Song
text:
and suddenly life

in my poor man's plate

a lean piece of heavenly pig

here on my plate

watching me

watching you

or killing a fly without malice

annihilating the light

or making it

making it

like someone who opens his eyes and chooses

a sky overflowing

in the empty plate

Rubens plus onions

plus tears

so many stories

black indigestible miracles

and the star of the East

sandwiched in

and the bones of love

so gnawed and so hard

shining on another plate

this hunger of my own

exists

it is the soul's desire

which is the body

it is the rose of fat

that grows old

in its fleshly heaven

mea culpa, clouded eye

mea culpa, black morsel

mea culpa, divine nausea

there is no one else here

in this empty plate

but me

devouring my eyes

and yours
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The fractured lineation, sacramental language, grotesque food imagery, and self-consuming close are preserved; the source typo ‘el huesos’ is regularized as ‘the bones.’

title: A Window
text:
I count my fingers again.

(The frozen flower, the unknown head that
stalks me unhooks itself and cries out),

I look at the walls and their round, swift fruits,
I calculate, add stones, ashes, clouds
and trees that chase men
and pearls torn from malignant ponds
or from black, buried lungs
and horribly alive.


The spider that descends at a human pace knows me,
it owns a corner of my face,
there it nests, there it sings, swollen and sweet
among its green silk and clusters.

Outside, the region where night grows,
I fear it,
where night grows and falls in thick drops,
in deadly flashes of lightning.

Outside, the heavy breath of the ox,
the old fever of red wings,
the night falling
like a dark spring upon a breast.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The parenthetical apparition, counting imagery, human-paced spider, and final spring-like fall of night are preserved.

title: The Poem Is My Body...
text:
the poem is my body

this, poetry

the tired flesh

sleep the sun

crossing deserts

the ends of the soul touch

and I remember you Dickinson

precious gentle ghost

wandering through time and distance

you dwell in the other's mouth

you fall into air you are the air

that strikes with invisible salt

my forehead

the ends of the soul touch

they close the earth is heard turning

that sound without light

blind sand beating us

so it will be eyes that were a mouth

that spoke hands that open

and close empty

far away in your window

you watch the wind pass

you see yourself pass your face aflame

posthumous star of summer

and you fall made into a bird

made into snow in the fountain

on the earth in oblivion

and you return with a false woman's name

with your winter clothes

with your white clothes of

winter

in mourning
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The lowercase, fragmentary lineation, address to Dickinson, and metamorphic ending are preserved; ‘errando’ is rendered as the deliberately open ‘wandering.’

title: Auvers-sur-Oise
text:
No one is going to open the door for you. Keep knocking.

Insist.

On the other side, music can be heard. No. It is the telephone bell.

You are mistaken.

It is the noise of machines, an electric panting, squeals,
whiplashes.

No. It is music.

No. Someone is crying very slowly.

No. It is a sharp shriek, an enormous, very high tongue licking the
pale and empty sky.

No. It is a fire.


All riches, all miseries, all men, all things disappear in that burning melody.

You are alone, on the other side.

They do not want to let you in.

Search, search again, climb, scream. It is useless.

Be the transparent little worm, curled up, insignificant.

With your mortal little eyes, go around the block, measure with your murky,
warm belly its impregnable roundness.

You, little worm, worm-mouth, worm-ear, master of death and life.

You cannot enter.

They say.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The escalating mishearings, imperative sequence, diminutive worm imagery, and isolated closing “They say” are preserved.

title: Before Me, That Lunar Face...
text:
Before me, that lunar face.

Silver nose, birds on the forehead.


Birds on the forehead?


And then there is red

and everything the earth forgets.

Moisture with the powers of fire

flowering behind the black eyelashes.

A face on the wall.

Behind the wall, beyond every will,

farther still than looking and keeping silent:

what?


Is there always something to break, abolish, or fear?

And on the other side? In reverse?


The hand flies, the line is born,

vibrant destiny, black destiny.

For an instant the melody is clear,

the afternoon seems eternal,

the shadow of the sky utterly pure.


I return once more. I ask.

Perhaps that silence says something,

it is an immense letter that names and contains us

in its deep air.

Perhaps the death behind that smile

is love, a gigantic love

in whose center we burn.


Perhaps the other side exists

and is also the gaze

and all this is the other

and that is this

and we are a form that changes with the light

until we are only light, only shadow.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The recursive questions, lunar face, and reversals of other side/this side are preserved; the source typo ‘ínea’ is repaired to the clear ‘line.’

title: Out of Time
text:
I


The day went away,

the scales of sleep turn.

Everything descends,

the night is tedium.

In the desert, in darkness,

afraid of love

the oyster weeps alone.


Pale leaves fall from your brow,

You move away, black bubble without a destiny.

A thousand streets suddenly open,

reefs in flames hold your body

frozen like a tear,

nothing hurts you,

the coral drives its claw into your shadow,

your blood slides,

floods meadows,

jumps from windows

like a red sound

and all this is nothing but autumn.


II


The lightning has perfumed

our house fiercely.

We are thirsty, we are in a hurry

to strike with the bone

of a flower in the darkness.

There is a felled tree in this story.

We contemplate the sky.

There are no signs.

It is day

It is night

The spider that measured time has died,

There is only an old wall

and a new family

of shadows.


All the inexplicable pallor

is memory.

Crossing from wall to wall,

the abyss is the eyelid,

there the world is shipwrecked,

ravaged by a tear.


I wake.

First island of consciousness:

a tree.

Fear invents flight.

The familiar desert receives me.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The two-part structure, abrupt capitalization, seasonal metamorphoses, and final consciousness/desert image are preserved.
